notes.meaning: Joshua got up early in the morning and led all Israel from Shittim to the edge of the Jordan River. He did not look for an easier path or delay his duty, but moved forward promptly in faith. The camp rested there before crossing, trusting God to open a way through the water.

After three days of waiting by the river, officers went through the camp to give the people their final orders. This brief pause gave families and herds time to get ready, while also letting the whole nation look at the swollen river and realize they needed God's help. Waiting on God prepares our hearts to see Him work.

The officers told the people to move out of their positions and follow the ark of the covenant when the priests carried it forward. The ark was a sacred golden chest that served as the visible sign of God's presence and His covenant promise to Israel. In earlier travels the ark stayed in the middle of the camp, but now God Himself went out in front to lead them.

The people were told to stay about a thousand yards behind the ark and not come too close. This distance showed deep respect for God's holiness, and it allowed the entire crowd to keep their eyes on the ark as their guide. Because they had never traveled through this riverbed before, they needed to follow God step by step.

Joshua commanded the people to consecrate themselves because the Lord was going to do wonders among them the next day. To consecrate means to set oneself apart from ordinary tasks and sins by washing and focusing the mind completely on God. When we expect God to act, we should prepare our hearts with reverence and obedience.

Joshua told the priests to take up the ark and march out ahead of the whole nation. The priests obeyed at once, stepping out front without yet seeing how the deep waters would make way for them. Leaders are called to set an example of courage by trusting God's direction before the path is clear.

The Lord spoke to Joshua and promised to begin exalting him in the sight of all the people that very day. Just as God had proved Moses was His chosen leader at the Red Sea, He was now going to prove that His power was with Joshua at the Jordan. God honors those who faithfully serve Him and obey His word.

God commanded Joshua to tell the priests carrying the ark to stop and stand still once they reached the edge of the river. They were to walk right to the brink of the flooded waters and hold their ground. Their steady obedience at the water's edge was the first step in setting the miracle in motion.

Joshua called the Israelites together to listen to the words of the Lord their God. He made sure the people heard God's promises before they witnessed the miracle, so that their trust would rest on God's spoken word. Hearing God's word prepares us to recognize His works.

Joshua announced that this miracle would prove the living God was actively present among them. Unlike the dead, powerless idols of neighboring nations, the true God has life and the power to drive out all seven Canaanite tribes. Crossing the river dry-shod was God's guarantee that He would give them total victory in the land.

The ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth was to lead the people straight into the river. God is called the Lord of all the earth because all rivers and natural elements are entirely under His sovereign rule. Knowing that the Master of creation walked before them gave Israel boldness to move forward.

Joshua told the people to choose twelve men, with one leader representing each tribe of Israel. Although their specific job was not explained yet, they were selected early so they would be ready for a special task in the dry riverbed. God often prepares people ahead of time for the work He wants them to do.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers such as Gregory of Nyssa saw the twelve chosen men and their stones as pointing forward to the twelve apostles who would minister Christian baptism.

notes.meaning: Joshua promised that as soon as the priests carrying the ark stepped into the Jordan, the waters flowing down from above would be cut off and rise up in a heap. The river would not freeze by cold weather or drain away slowly, but stop instantly by divine power. God waited for their feet to touch the water before showing His mighty hand.

The people packed up their tents to make the crossing, while the priests carried the ark of the covenant out ahead of them. Leaving their camp and marching toward a flooded river took real trust in God's promises. True faith moves forward in obedience even when obstacles seem impossible.

The Jordan was overflowing its banks, which happened every spring during harvest because melted snow rushed down from the northern mountains. In spite of the dangerous flood, the priests walked straight down to the edge until their feet dipped into the water. God chose the most difficult season of the year so His power would be unmistakable.

The moment the priests stepped into the water, the river stopped flowing from upstream and piled up miles away near the city of Adam. The water heading south to the Salt Sea drained completely away, leaving a dry riverbed right opposite Jericho. God cleared a wide, safe path for His people to march straight into the promised land.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars treat the story as a legendary memory designed to shape Israel's national identity rather than an exact historical event, noting that the Jordan often carried symbolic meaning for the nation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Church teachers saw the waters rolling back as a picture of baptism, where a believer's old nature is turned back and washed clean by God's grace.

notes.meaning: The priests carrying the ark stood firmly on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan until the entire nation had safely crossed over. The ark stayed in the riverbed as a shield, showing that the same divine power that stopped the river was keeping them safe. God faithfully preserves His people until their journey through danger is complete.

differ.view: Preachers like Charles Spurgeon saw crossing the Jordan as a picture of a Christian passing through death into the rest of heaven.
Some evangelicals reject comparing the crossing to heaven because Canaan was full of battles and sin, seeing it instead as a picture of entering into spiritual victory by faith.
Lutheran teachers often highlight the crossing as a foreshadowing of baptism, where Jesus, as the true ark and greater Joshua, leads believers through the waters into God's kingdom.
